newsitem.title: USA: Vacations for body and spirit give more bang for buck.
newsitem.headline: Vacations for body and spirit give more bang for buck.

text.p: How many of us have enjoyed a vacation, only to find its restful effects diminished within days, or even hours, of returning to work?
A resort vacation can delightful in the short run, but after the photos are developed and the sun tan fades, there's often little to remember.

But combine a resort setting with programmes designed to enrich the body, soul or intellect, and you may end up getting something of long-lasting value at a price no greater than your budget can afford.

"Vacations like this are not necessarily cheap, but they will last all your life," said Ellen Lederman, author of the new book, "Vacations That Can Change Your Life" (Sourcebooks, November 1996, $16.95).
"Work only goes so far. It doesn't give a lot of personal satisfaction," said Lederman, a counsellor and occupational therapist in Alpharetta, Ga., an Atlanta suburb.

Often in a bucolic or a resort-like setting, many run by not-for-profit organisations, vacationers can participate in typical activites such as sports, swimming or hiking while learning life-long skills, such as a language, meditation or conflict resolution.
Lederman breaks adventure, workshop or retreat vacations into five very flexible categories: holistic, spiritual, health and healing, self-imporovement and learning.
Holistic vacations integrate mind, body and spirit. Vacationers can take classes in such things as dream interpretation, eating disorders and assertiveness training in resort-like settings.
"This is different from a spa in that it is a lot less passive," she said. "Here, (a vacationer) is actively engaged in change ... You don't say 'do for me' as you would at a spa.
"Here, you're learning ways to change your life, and change in the future."
Examples of this type of vacation are Eselen Institute, Big Sur, Calif. (408-667-3000) and another well known example is Disney Institute in Orlando, Fla. (800-496-6337).
A spiritual vacation would be a religious retreat, with accommodations ranging from the simple at a monestary or ashram, to the more lavish at a resort.
"It gives you a chance to regroup -- go into a beautiful setting and get yourself together," Lederman said.
On a healing and health-promoting vacation, "weight reduction goes beyone fat farms -- it's not just a quick fix," she said.
Several run by the Seventh Day Adventist Church offer vegetarian diets and exercise but are "more supportive than a spa." One such area is the Wildwood Lifestyle Centre, Wildwood, Ga. (800-634-9355).

Self-improvement vacations offer the opportunity to build or improve relationships. Most vacations provide the time to focus on the individual, such as classes in assertiveness training, goal setting or stress reduction.

The Option Institute and Fellowship, in Sheffield, Mass., (413-229-2100) was founded by a father of an autistic boy. Here, people go for a week to better their communications skills and, hopefully, become more able to cope with the ups and downs of life.
Learning vacations combine the relaxation of a traditional vacation with the opportunity to learn a new skill, such as a foreign language, filmmaking, dramatic arts or writing.
At Camp Winnarainbow in Berkeley, Calif. (510-525-4304), the study of circus skills and performing arts helps build self-confidence, Lederman said.

The Rowe Camp and Conference Centre in Rowe, Mass., (413-339-4954), run by the Unitarian Universalist Church, is a holistic summer camp for adults and children, where among other activities, visitors can take classes in how to laugh.
Lederman said that on average a value-added vacation will cost about $100 a day, including accommodations, classes and meals.

However, since many of the resorts are run by not-for-profit organisations, prospective visitors should ask if scholarships are available. Also, some may offer work/study programmes, where a reduction in fees might be given in exchange for gardening, meal preparation or office duties.
When selecting a vacation of this type, Lederman suggests that visitors do a bit of research and read brochures to get a feel for what is offered and to whom the centre is geared.
"This book is just the first step in determining what kind of vacation to take," she said.
To order "Vacations That Can Change Your Life," call Sourcebooks at 1-800-43-BRIGHT (274448).
